transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 10:00 AM PT / 17:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (BrightCart EM), Marco Ruiz (BrightCart ML Eng), Priya Nair (BrightCart CTO)

Summary:
Quick sync on week-10 POC caching results; reviewed prefix/KV cache hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, observed cache skew and eviction behavior; agreed on next benchmarking steps, instrumentation additions, and tentative pilot timeline.

Topics:
- KV cache hit rates and prefix reuse
- Warmup and prompt deduping strategies
- Eviction policy and TTL tuning
- Metrics and dashboards to share
- Next-step benchmarks and PRD for pilot rollout

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: All right, good morning everyone thanks for joining our weekly caching sync. Quick roll call, we got Aisha, Marco, Priya from BrightCart, and Liam and me from Redwood. How's everyone doing?
[00:18] Aisha: Doing good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see the numbers.
[00:22] Marco: Yep, excited. We ran the bigger run last night and I have some initial numbers.
[00:27] Sophie: Great, that's what we'll focus on. Liam, wanna take the floor on the Redwood-side summary?
[00:32] Liam: Sure. So high level: after last week's config change (increasing KV cache window and enabling prefix normalization), the measured overall KV hit rate moved from roughly 12% to ~46% on the staging traffic sample. That brought token cost down and tail latency improved for cached requests. Caveat: distribution is very skewed - the top 5% of prefixes account for ~72% of hits.
[01:00] Priya: Interesting, so a small prefix set is doing most of the heavy lifting. Is that expected given your traffic?
[01:08] Marco: We suspected that, yeah. A lot of our UI templates and a few high-frequency product-description prompts are repetitive. But we also have long-tail personalized prompts which barely hit.
[01:18] Sophie: That's the classic mix. We should separate warm/warmable prefixes vs cold personalized ones. Key question for the POC: at what cache size/eviction policy do you get diminishing returns for cost reduction?
[01:30] Aisha: Also curious about correctness — did you see any stale/incorrect outputs because of prefix reuse? We have some prompts that include dynamic user context.
[01:39] Liam: Good point. We added stricter prefix hashing that includes intent markers, and we disabled caching for any prompt containing the placeholder "{user_recent_activity}". We didn't observe stale responses in the sample, but the QA is ongoing.
[01:49] Marco: On the numbers — breakdown: total requests 2.1M over 24h sample, unique prefixes ~520k, avg tokens per prefix ~42, median TTL we used was 10 minutes for KV entries. Hit-rate by bucket: top 1% prefixes 54% hit-rate, 1-5% bucket 28%, long-tail buckets <5% each.
[02:15] Priya: That makes sense — most of our traffic is concentrate on category pages. So from ROI perspective we should tune to capture that top 5% cheaply.
[02:24] Sophie: Agreed. We recommended increasing the reserved cache memory for the pilot to 64GB and switching the eviction to LFU for this workload. That should keep hot prefixes around longer than LRU.
[02:36] Marco: Can you remind me the memory per key assumptions? Last week numbers were fuzzy.
[02:41] Liam: We estimate payload per cached KV entry at ~1.2 KB (prompt prefix + metadata + pointer to KV). So 64GB roughly stores ~55M entries in idealized estimate, real-world overhead drops that to ~40M. Given your unique prefixes of ~520k that's plenty headroom to keep the hot set in memory.
[03:02] Aisha: Wait 1.2 KB seems small — do you factor in vector pointers or serialization overhead?
[03:07] Liam: This is the raw prefix + small metadata. If you include large serialized key blobs or embeddings we count separately; we are not caching embeddings, just prefix strings and model state pointers for autoregressive reuse.
[03:18] Marco: One oddity we saw: after enabling prefix normalization, a subset of prefixes that we expected to consolidate didn't because of small template variations — punctuation, trailing whitespace. Might need more aggressive normalization or a template registry.
[03:33] Sophie: Good call — we can add a light-weight canonicalization step in the preprocessor (strip punctuation, normalize whitespace, lower-case for non-proper nouns) as an optional flag. We'll include that in the config spreadsheet.
[03:45] Priya: Any latency regressions for cache misses?
[03:49] Liam: Miss latency remains similar to baseline. The wins are on cached requests where we see 35-50% lower tail latency (p95/p99 depending on token length). There is some overhead for cache lookups (~2-5ms) but it's amortized vs the decode cost.
[04:05] Marco: We also instrumented KV cache hit time series; it spikes during certain cron jobs which flood prefix variety. That impacts hit-rate temporarily, so maybe we need to treat ingestion windows differently.
[04:17] Aisha: Could we prioritize cache warming for known high-traffic pages after deployments?
[04:21] Liam: Yes — warmup strategy is on our list: incremental prefill for top-N prefixes, plus a background async warmup that runs during low-traffic windows. We can add an API to push warm keys from your side.
[04:33] Sophie: We'll add a 'warm keys' endpoint as a pilot feature. Marco, would you be able to push a list of top 10-50 prefixes you want warmed?
[04:42] Marco: Yep, can do that. We'll extract from analytics and share.
[04:45] Priya: On the correctness front again — are there safety checks to avoid serving cached completions when user-specific context changed? We had one incident in the lower environment where the cache returned a generic offer that didn't match the user's locale.
[04:58] Liam: We recommend including contextual keys for locale/session when appropriate. There's also a policy to mark certain tokens as non-cacheable; we can include those rules in the config. For offers specifically, add a locale tag to the prefix hash.
[05:09] Sophie: Great, that will be in the config doc.
[05:12] Aisha: Any thoughts about TTL? 10 minutes felt arbitrary.
[05:16] Liam: We tried 10 minutes as conservative starting point. For product descriptions that rarely change, you could set TTL to hours/days. For dynamic user-context prompts, TTL should be near-zero or disabled. We recommend per-prefix TTL metadata.
[05:28] Marco: Would love to see LRU vs LFU comparison — you mentioned LFU might be better for our skewed workload.
[05:33] Liam: We'll run both in the test harness. Action: I will add LFU/LRU comparison for metrics and push a dashboard link.
[05:40] Sophie: Quick note about cost math — with the improved 46% hit rate, your modeled token spend reduction is ~22% on the sample. That's in the spreadsheet I'll share.
[05:50] Priya: That aligns with expectations. If we can get hit rate to 60% on the top buckets that's a material saving.
[05:57] Marco: We also saw occasional cache churn related to small template changes between mobile/web. Are you able to canonicalize across devices?
[06:05] Liam: We can add a per-channel mapping to normalize known device template variants. It's more config than code.
[06:11] Aisha: Good. On the instrumentation side, what new metrics will you expose? We need hit-rate by prefix-bucket, hit-rate per endpoint, eviction count, avg TTL, and miss latency percentiles.
[06:23] Sophie: We'll provide a telemetry dashboard with those panels. Also include a CSV export for your finance team.
[06:30] Marco: Awesome. Can you also include sample request/response traces for some cached vs uncached flows? That helped us debug earlier.
[06:37] Liam: Yes, we will include sample traces with obfuscated PII.
[06:42] Sophie: A couple of low-level questions from Marco earlier — are you saving KV cache keys to disk persistently across restarts?
[06:49] Liam: For Dedicated/private pilot we support snapshotting to local SSD with recovery; for hosted the runtime keeps an in-memory working set and optional periodic snapshots to a customer-controlled durable store. We'll document the snapshot cadence and recovery time.
[07:02] Priya: For compliance, we'll need to show that PII never gets cached; is there an opt-out list?
[07:09] Liam: Yes, we support regex filters to mark prompts as non-cacheable and also a flag to scrub detected PII before any cache key generation. We'll include that in the security docs.
[07:18] Sophie: We'll attach the security checklist and SOC 2 notes.
[07:22] Aisha: Great. Any blockers on our side to run the 100k benchmark?
[07:27] Marco: I just need the harness and the warm key list — should be straightforward. We'll run it on Thursday.
[07:33] Sophie: Perfect. To summarize action items...
[07:36] Sophie: Redwood: share cache tuning spreadsheet, LFU/LRU comparison dashboard, warm-keys API doc, security checklist. BrightCart: run 100k benchmark with warmup and share results, generate top prefixes list, review TTL choices. We'll reconvene next week same time.
[07:55] Priya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:58] Aisha: Thanks.
[08:00] Marco: Thanks all.
[08:02] Sophie: Thanks folks, end of sync.
